newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Emotional welcome home for Romania's exiled king.
newsitem.headline: Emotional welcome home for Romania's exiled king.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael, tears streaming down his face, returned to his homeland on Friday, his citizenship restored by a new government enlisting his prestige to enhance its longshot bid for quick NATO entry.
Michael, 75, was visibly shaken as he stepped down from a commercial aircraft at Bucharest's Otopeni airport to be mobbed on the tarmac by several hundred well-wishers.
He embraced his wife, Ana of Bourbon Parma, and choked back tears in a ceremony beamed live to Romania's 23 million people.
The king's five-day visit, his second to Romania since the 1989 fall of communism, is described as private and he has promised to abide by the 1991 republican constitution.

Michael picked his way through the profusion of television crews, government ministers and prominent cultural figures thronging the airport's VIP lounge. He thanked an unidentified official who handed him a new Romanian passport and waved to the crowd before getting into a waiting car.
Well-wishers chanted "The monarchy will save Romania!" and "King Michael, King Michael!". A large portrait of the king, forced to abdicate by pro-Moscow communists in 1947, was carried aloft.
"This marks the end of political exile for Romanians," said Doru Braia, a former refugee who returned home from Germany after Ceausescu's overthrow. "The king was the last exile."
His motorocade paused at a shrine by the airport marking the spot where dozens of Romanian soldiers died in the 1989 upheaval which toppled Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

It then proceeded to the Villa Elisabeta, a former royal residence where he signed his abdication at gunpoint 50 years ago. A crowd of about 1,000, many with Romanian flags bearing Michael's portrait, craned for a glimpse at the monarch.
He was later to lay a wreath in University Square, site of clashes with protesters during the 1989 revolution.
President Emil Constantinescu says he will invite the king to dinner next Tuesday at what was once a royal palace.
He is also to lunch with Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea and centrist government ministers who restored his citizenship a week ago in what was termed an "act of reparation".

Constantinescu has suggested Michael could use his influence to win an early entry ticket to an enlarged NATO alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Six NATO members, he argues, are constitutional monarchies.
Many Romanians revere Michael for his courage as a young monarch during World War Two, when he arrested fascist leader Marshal Ion Antonescu and switched Romania to the Allied side.
On his first return from Switzerland in 1992, Michael drew hundreds of thousands into the streets on Orthodox Easter.

His subsequent visits were blocked by ex-communist president Ion Iliescu, who treated him as a foreign commoner and made the granting of a visa contingent on his public acceptance of the constitution.

His public reception this time is likely to be more low-key than in 1992, with a government favourable to him in power and many Romanians preoccupied with plunges in living standards which have left them far behind other east European states.
Only a small fraction of Romanians favour restoration of the king, though one of two small monarchist parties is within the ruling coalition.
The ex-communists, thrown into opposition last year, have denounced the visit as an attempt to distract Romanians from price rises for utilities and staples introduced this month.
And nationalist parties have also criticised it as leaving the door open for constitutional ambiguity.
